description: Model validation techniques are critically important in data science work. Here, Nate Silver tests the empirical distribution of US election polling against what we would expect based on  the expected numerical distribution. #กรีนสกรีน  #datascience #datascientist #dataanalytics #2024elections #datasciencetok #statistics
hashtags: กรีนสกรีน, datascience, datascientist, dataanalytics, 2024elections, datasciencetok, statistics
_transcript: Nate Silver just came out with a pretty bombshell report suggesting that is almost guaranteed that the U.S. polling data is incorrect. In fact, he argues the probability that the U.S. election polling data is correct is less than 1 in 9 trillion. Now, he is using a data model validation technique that if you're a data scientist and you're running some fairly complicated models with weightings and different covariates and structures, this is really good practice. Now, there have been thousands of U.S. election polls in the United States, and they tend to have a margin of error of around like plus or minus 3 or 4 percentage points. But because this is essentially a one-to-one matchup, being plus or minus 3 points means that it should be a 6 percentage point gap between the two candidates. Right, so if they're actually tied, but you get a plus 3 errors per se like Kamala Harris, that takes away 3 from Donald Trump, and so the gap should be about 6. So when you think about a polling's margin of error or a confidence interval when you're doing a statistical model is that under repeated sampling, so if you repeat this experiment or if you repeat these polls and these surveys like over and over again, you should get a distribution of results that covers the span of this margin of error. So if the race was tied, you should get polls that are effectively normally distributed around a zero gap, but where there are outliers of plus 3, minus 3. And what Nate showed was if given the sample sizes of these polls, we should have seen no more than 55% of the polls being within 2.5 percentage points if the race was actually tied. So if the race was tied, we would expect to see the maximum number of close polls, right? So we don't even have to worry about the fact of the cases where they're not tied. But if the case was tied, we should see no more than 55% of the polls being within 2.5%. But in reality, we're seeing more than 80% of the polls that are being within plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. And given the number of polls and the sample size of these polls, Nate estimates the probability of this happening by random chance alone would be only 1 in 9.5 trillion. So the problem here is that it's really easy to lie with statistics, and this comes up with data scientists all the time when we're dealing with our stakeholders that basically want to hear the results that they want to hear. So these pollsters are going out and they're surveying people, but then they apply weights, and the weights are determined via a likely voter model that they have complete control over. So if they get a result that should be a normal outlier in random sampling that says, you know, Harris is up plus 4 or Trump is up plus 4, they will put their finger on the scale and they'll adjust these likely voter models so that it comes out closer to plus 1, minus 1 in either direction. And so what we're seeing here is that the empirical distribution of polling results is not what we would expect based on characteristics of the normal distribution and of the surveys and the sample sizes, and that is a huge red flag that there is a problem with the polling.

_transcript: Tomorrow is the U.S. presidential election. As always, there's a lot of debate on whether polls and forecasts can accurately predict the outcome. Nate Silver, the founder of FiveThirtyEight, and Nassib Tlaib, a former quant and author known for his works on uncertainty, have publicly debated the best approach for predicting these outcomes. Tlaib suggests using a finance-based perspective. If you give odds for some outcome, you should be willing to transact at the price those odds imply. Let me give you an example. Let's say I think the Newark Jets have a 75% chance of beating the Arizona Cardinals next week in the NFL game. This implies a fair money-line bet of minus $133 on the Jets and plus $400 on the Cardinals. This price is fair because I am willing to take either side of the bet. The higher payout for the Cardinals balances out the worse odds and vice versa for the Jets. In finance, this fair price is crucial. It prevents opportunities for arbitrage in markets. Tlaib argues that election predictions should meet this same standard. He takes issue with how forecasters may leave room for arbitrage by allowing large swings in odds. Now this setup has a parallel in finance, a financial derivative called a digital option. This contract pays 1 if an asset ends up above a set strike price and 0 if not. Here think of the asset's price as the vote share and the strike price as the win threshold. Now here's the interesting point. As uncertainty or volatility increases for the digital option, the price of the digital option will tend to 0.5 or a half, implying even odds for either side of the bet. Now the interesting thing is this is true no matter the current level of the asset price and no matter the strike price. Here's a plot demonstrating that for various digital option contracts. So as election day approaches and uncertainty grows, the prediction should theoretically hover around 50-50 odds, making it a coin toss. You can actually see this play out with how election betting odds have moved over the past few days. What we can take from this is that if anyone assumes to know exactly what the outcome of the selection is going to be, they are not actually taking into account of true uncertainty.

description: With the midterm elections now less than a year away, a new PBS News/NPR/Marist poll has signs of hope for Democrats and a few red flags for Republicans. Amna Nawaz and NPR's Domenico Montanaro break down the numbers and discuss what's resonating with voters. #pbsnewshour #newshour #pbsnews #politics #midterms #elections #npr #marist #democrat #republican
hashtags: pbsnewshour, newshour, pbsnews, politics, midterms, elections, npr, marist, democrat, republican
_transcript: With the midterm elections now less than a year away, a new PBS News-NPR-Marist poll has signs of hope for Democrats and a few red flags for Republicans. So what is resonating with voters? NPR senior political editor and correspondent Domenico Montanaro is here to break down the numbers. Good to see you. Hey, good to see you. Let's jump in. So Democrats came off some big election wins in New Jersey and New York City and Virginia a couple of weeks ago. Seems like they have an advantage. Midterms are still a long way off. But what does the poll show? And in a lot of places across the country, up and down the ballot, really. And I think that what this poll shows is that Democrats have a huge advantage right now. And the real issue is because of affordability. But what the poll shows is by 55 to 41 margin, Democrats, people say that they would pick a Democrat in their district if the midterm elections were held today. Now, why is that important? It's a plus 14 advantage on what's known as the congressional ballot. When you have that large of a lead, it is really indicative of a potential wave. I mean, if you look back to 2022, for example, Democrats had only between an average of zero to four points. They lost nine seats in 2018. Democrats had an advantage between six and 12 points in our poll, and they obviously won big 40 seat advantage. Now, most people don't expect that we're going to see a wave of that kind next year. But right now starts out with Democrats with a big advantage. And a big piece of that is because of independents and how they've slid away. I mean, a 61 to 28 percent margin, independents say that they would pick a Democrat. These are major red flags and warning signs for the Republican Party right now. And we know a lot can happen in the next year. But that also includes whatever happens on this redistricting front. We've seen efforts by President Trump and the Republicans, counter efforts by the Democrats in California. This is all tied up in the courts right now. But does any of this make the Democratic polling advantage moot? You know, it depends on how this winds up shaking out. But frankly, we're seeing some evidence in the past week or so that this could boomerang on Republicans potentially. You know, Trump wanted to get five seats out of Texas. A court this week said that Texas's maps got to go back to the drawing board. Now, eventually they might get what they want, but they're also banking a lot on Latinos in South Texas having moved toward Donald Trump. And what we're seeing in our polling in the elections is that Latinos have really slid away from Donald Trump and Republicans. They moved over because of affordability. And what we're hearing from a lot of those voters is that they don't feel that Trump has done enough to address lowering costs and that they are upset with how he's approached deportations in this country, feeling like, you know, they were OK with supporting criminals, but not OK with deporting people in their communities in the same way that they see it being conducted. And like we've talked about, prices are the real issue, right? I mean, when you look at the issues inside our poll, 57 percent say that lowering prices should be the administration's top priority. Nothing else comes close. You can see there immigration, 16 percent in second. And even a plurality of Republicans there say that lowering prices should be Trump's top priority. Meanwhile, if you look at the Republican Party, we have seen some rifts. We've been covering Marjorie Taylor Greene's break with the president, him calling her a traitor. But how are Americans looking at the president's performance right now? Yeah, I think that this is a huge reason why maybe there's an opening for other Republicans to show some independence. I think they're going to be watching what happens with Marjorie Taylor Greene to see if she suffers any political consequences, as Trump says that she will. If she doesn't, I wonder what that's going to mean as Trump continues to look further and further like a lame duck and is on the wrong side of these issues. In the polling here, only 39 percent say that they approve of the job that Trump is doing. And when you look inside the numbers, only 24 percent of independents approve of the job he's doing. Now, the other number, as you see, nine in 10 Republicans still sticking with the president. So it continues to put Republican candidates in a vice, because we're seeing that when Trump is not on the ballot, Republican MAGA base voters don't necessarily show up. We heard from a lot of Republican voters in this poll who said that they are pro-Trump, but they're not necessarily voting for Republican candidates. That is a real problem for them, because they need to be able to show some independence from Trump to be able to say, to appeal to those crossover voters and to independents. But they can't alienate the base. Can I ask you quickly about one more thing we saw in here? Some bigger frustrations among American voters with political institutions and beyond. What do you take away from that? People don't like anything. If you look at what they think about the confidence in institutions, really bad numbers here for almost everybody, including us in the media, by the way, only 25 percent approve of what we're doing. Full results, of course, always available online. Domenico Montanaro, NPR, always good to see you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

_transcript: Little less than half of New Yorkers, 48 percent, approve of Mayor Zora Mamdani's job performance in these first 100 days. This is 14 points lower than what former Mayor Eric Adams was polling at during the same time. But polling director Lee Mieringoff says these numbers are still a good start. I think part of it has to do with the fact that he's relatively new on the political scene, but we do find in the numbers kind of like a newfound optimism in the city, where overwhelmingly people felt the city was headed in the wrong direction. And now with Mamdani, there's a new trajectory. People think it's heading in the right direction. As Mieringoff points out, a majority of New Yorkers in this mayor's poll do think that Mamdani is hardworking and changing New York City for the better. Sixty percent of New Yorkers polled also believe Mamdani is fulfilling his campaign promises. Mamdani did deliver on appointing members to the rent guidelines board who agree with his rent freeze, and he got the ball rolling on free child care for some two-year-olds in the city starting later this year. But he did shift slightly on other promises made, like expanding the city's housing voucher program, which he's now trying to stop in court. And he also seems to be backing away Slee from his push to get rid of the NYPD's gang database. Professor and political analyst JC Polanco says in his view, this is a good thing. His campaign promises are not realistic. However, this is the truth. His base wants to see the fight. His base wants to see him fight for it, understanding that they're lofty, unrealistic. There's a cult of personality when it comes to Mayor Mamdani, very similar to President Trump in that regard, in that people want to make sure he's happy, especially in his party. _transcript: President Trump's hardline immigration policies have earned mixed reviews from Americans. That's according to our latest PBS News NPR Marist poll released today. To walk us through some of the new numbers, I'm joined now by NPR's Domenico Montanaro. Great to see you. Hey, great to be with you. Let's pick up on immigration that Laura was just reporting on. It was a central issue for Mr. Trump's re-election campaign. How do voters look at this issue at this point in his presidency? Well, his handling of immigration mirrors his overall job approval rating. Only 43% say that they approve of the job that the president is doing when it comes to handling immigration. 52% disapprove. And like I said, that's the same number as approve and disapprove of him overall. He doesn't get really good marks on almost anything either. Only 41% approve of his job on foreign policy and just 39% on the economy. So immigration's the best of those, but still not great. Domenico, like a lot of issues, it gets more interesting the deeper you go. Our colleague Josh Barajas spoke to a number of voters about the president's immigration agenda. One, a man named Stephen Singh, who's an independent voter in California, had this to say. I would love a more streamlined pathway to citizenship for immigrants. I don't wanna see students deported. I hate to see students being deported as a weapon to spread someone's political ideals and to silence others. So the nuanced answer is there are some cases where I think his immigration policy is spot on and there's some where I think it's overstepping the bounds. Is that view showing up in the polling? Yeah, I mean, in reality, views of immigration are much more nuanced than sometimes the political debate lends itself to be. Republicans feel very strongly one way, Democrats feel very strongly another way. When we look directly at deportation policies and whether or not they're making the country more safe, less safe, or not having any impact, you can see they're 43% say that Trump's deportation policies are making the country safer, 33% say less safe, a quarter say no impact at all. When it comes to how that breaks down by party, as we were talking about, 81% of Republicans think that his policies are making the country safer. Only 17% of Democrats are with just 34% of independents as well saying that they think that his policies are making the country safer. And when it comes to who is being impacted and targeted in these policies, how do Americans view that? And reflecting a lot of what we heard that voter say there, there's a real range. There's a wide range here. When it comes to violent offenders, people who are convicted of crimes who are in the country without permanent legal status, 80% say deport them. When it comes to nonviolent offenders, those convicted of crimes but nonviolent crimes, almost 6 in 10 also say to deport them as well. But it gets a lot trickier for Trump the further down we go. We heard that person talk about those who have overstayed visas. Only 49% say that they should be deported, real split in the country. And when it comes to those industry workers, people in the food and agricultural industry, for example, 44% say that they should be deported. A majority say don't do that. So we've seen a number of these immigration policies, other policies of the president, ending up in court. There's a mixed bag in terms of where the rulings are landed. But there are questions being raised by the president and his supporters about whether or not the president needs to comply with those court orders. How do people feel about this issue? Well, overall, I mean, 82% of people said that they think that any president should follow court orders, even if he or she doesn't like them. When you dig a little bit deeper into those numbers, though, 22% of Republicans only said that they feel strongly about this, as opposed to big majorities of independents and Democrats who said strongly that they think a president should follow this. So I guess if there's something they really don't like, they might be able to give Trump a little bit of leash. Here's the other thing that stuck out to me. Going into Independence Day, the poll showed a striking number of people who say they are concerned about the state of democracy in America. What should we understand about that? description: On Sunday Hungarians go to the polls in the country's most important election in decades. But how is the winner decided? CGTN’s correspondent Pablo Gutierrez explains. #Hungary #Election
_transcript: Hungary is heading into one of the most important elections in its modern history. And to understand what is at stake, you first need to understand how the system works. Here, voters don't just cast one vote, they cast two. One vote goes to the local candidates in their district. The other one goes to a national party list. It's a system designed to blend two worlds, local representation and national power. But that balance is where everything gets complicated. Hungary's parliament has 199 seats. 106 are decided in individual districts. Whoever gets the most votes wins. Simple as that. The remaining 93 are distributed based on national party results using a proportional system. So even if a party wins the popular vote, it still needs to win across the map. Because this system rewards geography, not just popularity. And that's why this election is so tight. For the first time in years, the opposition is pulling ahead. But winning seats is what really counts. At its core, this election is about more than just numbers. It's about whether 16 years of leadership continues under Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and his Fidesz party. Or whether voters push for a change, the promise offered by Peter Magyar and his Tisza party. The system itself here in Hungary, shaped over the past decade, can favor parties that dominate districts, even without winning big nationally. So on election day, every vote matters. But where these votes are cast may matter even more. And from here in Budapest, you can feel it. A country watching closely, waiting to see which direction it chooses next.

They're often caught within minutes. The New York Times gets its election night results from the Associated Press, which combines data from state and county election offices with the work of thousands of correspondents across the country. The AP then checks those vote totals for any kind of inconsistencies. The Times also does its own verification process to look for any other inconsistencies or problems in the posted results. It's a meticulous process going through reporting results, but in the social media age, a simple screenshot of one of those errors can create a disinformation landscape and erode trust in the final results of an election. The last question is, why did one candidate appear to be ahead and then a lot of votes come in at the last second for the other candidate? We can go back to Pennsylvania in 2020 to see what happened there. They were inundated with mail ballots. That took a long time to count, and so on election night, most of the mail ballots from Democratic areas like Philadelphia and Pittsburgh had not yet been counted, so it looked like former President Trump was winning Pennsylvania. But as those ballots were counted over the next four days from Democratic areas, President Biden eventually caught up and the race was called for him. This delayed reporting results can sometimes lead to what are known as mirages, which is when it appears that a certain candidate is leading simply because more of their area's ballots have been counted and reported than the other candidates. The timing of results can sometimes simply come down to where votes were cast. In some states, rural areas are faster at uploading their results than urban areas. In some states, they report mail ballots instantly. In others, it could take well into the night or even in the coming days. And in some states, early in-person voting is all reported at once. So while it might be frustrating to not be able to know who won the presidential election or who controls Congress within hours of polls closing, this is just the system working as it should. And it's important to know that you're watching every vote be counted, and that's critical to a healthy democracy.

_transcript: The polling tells a different story than the election fundamentals, though. The 538 polling model gives Democrats an 80 percent chance of losing between two and 30 seats in the House and an 80 percent chance of either losing four seats or gaining two seats in the Senate. Meanwhile, the models over at The Economist give Democrats a five point higher chance of keeping a majority in the House at 23 percent and a two point lower chance of winning a majority in the Senate at 45 percent. This is considerably more optimistic for Democrats than the fundamentals. There are plenty of reasons why outcomes of this election might be less conventional than previous midterms, primarily because voter approval of both parties is low. On one hand, prevailing narratives around things like inflation aren't favorable for President Joe Biden, which trickles down to his party. On the other hand, the GOP has elevated underqualified extreme candidates on the backs of endorsements of Donald Trump, who himself is even more unpopular than President Biden. Most Republican candidates continue to lie about election fraud, and about 70 percent of Republicans polled agree with them. However, over 60 percent of independents polled agree that Biden was legitimately elected, a number that shows just how powerful authoritarianism in the United States has become, by the way. Likewise, only 30 percent of Americans polled approve of the Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade, and 74 percent of Democratic or Democratic leaning voters in anti-abortion states polled said that they were more motivated to vote now. More than 8 million new voters have aged into eligibility since the last election. These voters are significantly more diverse than the electorate, and they approve of President Biden at a much higher rate than the electorate. But it's harder to turn out first time voters because they haven't done it before. And the youth vote doesn't have even geographic distribution. There was a concern that he wouldn't go quietly, having built a system that made it very hard to defeat his Fidesz ruling party, but I think the scale of the defeat here, the projected scale of the defeat left him with no option but to accept the result. He gave his, he conceded defeat with just over half of the vote counted, which even at that stage the opposition Tisza party was projected to win a super majority, more than 135 seats in that building there behind me, Hungary's stunning parliament building, so a really really comprehensive defeat for his Fidesz party after 16 years as I say. He said he's congratulated the winning party, he says the election result is clear, he said it is painful for us and we will serve our nation from the opposition. I am at a watch party, kind of street party, organised by the opposition here on the banks of the Danube. The results are being played out on a big screen just out of your shot over my shoulder there and whenever a new result comes in in favour of the opposition a huge cheer goes up, there's a real party atmosphere here, people are popping champagne corks, they're here with their children to witness what promises to be a historic moment. And Ivor, talk to us about the run-up to this election result because a lot of the discussion in Hungary was about another country, wasn't it, about Ukraine and Zelensky. Yeah you're absolutely right, walking around Budapest this week and looking at the campaign posters you'd think that Vladimir Zelensky was running for office here because his face has been everywhere here, it's dominated the campaign posters of Viktor Orban's party, he's campaigned on a platform of fear, he is anti-Ukraine, pro-Russia and his posters warn that a vote for the opposition would be dragging Hungary into war against Russia. He casts his rival Peter Magyar as an agent of Ukraine, as an agent of Brussels, warmongers supposedly. He says this is a choice between war and peace, that he was the only one to keep Hungarians safe, the guardian of its security, sorry. But people clearly don't believe that, that kind of campaign, that platform of fear has not worked. The overwhelming message that we picked up here has been one, has been an appetite for change, people are just sick and tired and fed up of the corruption they want, there's failing public services here, deteriorating healthcare, long waits for medical procedures, there is a rising cost of living, food prices are going up, wages are falling, the economy is stagnating and people just want change. Those kind of platforms of fear have worked before with Orban's campaigns, campaigning eight years ago against mass immigration, four years against the spread of liberalism, George Soros was the kind of figure of hate then, but that platform of fear hasn't worked this time. It is a positive campaign that Peter Magyar, his rival has run, who is actually a former Orban insider, he emerged only two years ago, turning his back on Orban, launching his own campaign and in that time he's built a huge following, thanks largely to his youthful energy, a very savvy social media campaign, a very tireless campaign strategy as well, crisscrossing the country, visited all constituencies here and it's really resonated with people and people have got the change that they have so desperately desired.

For context, Farrah has historically been a safe Liberal seat, previously held by Susan Lee since 2001. So normally this wouldn't even be considered a competitive contest. But this by-election is different, because there is no incumbent. And the first poll of the race, a survey of about 1,200 people, shows a completely fragmented field. If One Nation verses Michelle Milthorpe, I suspect that One Nation will win, as Nationals voters will preference One Nation. If it's One Nation vs. the Nationals, I feel as if the Nationals will win because Michelle will likely preference the Nationals, but if it's the Nationals versus Michelle Milthorpe, I think it will be Michelle Milthorpe. This is because I feel like Michelle Milthorpe will have enough votes over the Nationals that even though One Nation will likely have preference for Michelle Milthorpe, I don't suspect it will quite be enough. Democrats are tasked with defending 23 of the 34 Senate seats up for election this November, including 8 of the 10 most competitive races and 3 seats in states that Donald Trump carried in both 2016 and 2020. This makes the 2024 Senate map highly favorable for Republicans. According to Decision Desk HQ's latest forecast, Republicans have a 71% chance of flipping the majority. And over on BetOnline, the prediction markets have Republicans favored at negative 350, which translates to a slightly better 75-80% chance of retaking control. Now let's dive into the latest polls across the most competitive Senate races to see if Republicans are on track to get the job done. With that said, let's start by filling out the safe seats for both parties, where their chance of winning is greater than 95%. For the Democrats, this includes Washington, California, and Hawaii, as well as New Mexico, Minnesota, New York, Vermont, Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Jersey, Delaware, and Virginia. Most of these states are also expected to vote for Kamala Harris by at least a 10-point margin at the top of the ticket. The only exceptions are Virginia and Minnesota. But in Minnesota, Democratic incumbent Amy Klobuchar is a proven electoral powerhouse, having been re-elected in 2018 with 60% of the vote, and she has never lost a race by less than 20 points. Similarly, in Virginia, Democratic Senator Tim Kaine won by 16 points in 2018 and has led his Republican challenger by double digits in every 2024 poll thus far. Now with these 14 safe states providing Democrats with a solid foundation at 42 Senate seats, it's hard to imagine them ending up with fewer than this number once all the votes are counted. On the Republican side, their safe states include North Dakota, Wyoming, and Utah, along with Nebraska's special election, Missouri, Tennessee, Mississippi, West Virginia, and Indiana. These are all solidly Republican states at the presidential level, with no unique factors making them competitive in this cycle. Notably, West Virginia will be a flip as Democratic incumbent Senator Joe Manchin is retiring, paving the way for GOP Governor Jim Justice to win by a landslide in November in this Trump-plus-40 state. You may also have noticed that I did not place Nebraska's regular election down as safe Republican. That's because a number of polls have come out recently showing independent candidate Dan Osborne within the margin of error or even outright leading Republican incumbent Senator Deb Fischer, who is pretty unpopular even within her own party. description: 64% of American Indian voters voted for trump? Nah. Lets take a closer look… #kamala #trump #election2024 #nbc #exitpolls #fyp #nativetiktok #nativeamerican #modernwarrior #greenscreen

_transcript: After the election, I was genuinely surprised to see NBC's exit poll results. It indicated that 64% of American Indian voters cast their ballot for Trump. Because I was confused, I decided to take a closer look and this is what I found. According to the 2020 US Census, there are 331 million people living in the United States. Of that number, there are only 3.7 million people who identified as American Indian or Alaskan Native, which is only 1% of the overall population. Now, the US Census Bureau has a demographic map that shows where American Indians live here in the United States. The darker the green, the higher the population rate. This is important because, based on the NBC exit poll data, they indicated that they interviewed people from 10 key states. And those states are Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Wisconsin. I took this list and reanalyzed the map provided by the US Census Bureau. And of all the states on that list, Arizona is the one with the largest American Indian population. So, I looked at the racial demographics of Arizona provided by NBC. Two things stand out. First, American Indian is not listed as a category, only other. And two, there's not enough data in the one key state that had the largest American Indian population. Because I was still confused, I did more digging and came across this article. Will Native voters support Harris or Trump? Two polls find two outcomes. A survey conducted by Northern Arizona University asked Native American voters in Arizona who they favored more for president, Kamala Harris or Donald Trump. And Harris led Trump by 35%, and she was polling at 64% over him, who stood at 29%. And there's this poll, conducted by Northwestern University's Metal School of Journalism, which was distributed by Native News Online, and asked Native people on a national scale who their choice was for president. The results showed that Trump came ahead at 44.8% compared to Kamala Harris, who came in at 37.44%. Now compare those two polls to NBC's, and the margins for favoring Trump are just drastically different. It just doesn't make sense, and I have three potential explanations as to why. One, major news outlets do not know how to accurately collect data regarding American slash Native American peoples. Just four years ago, CNN exit polls categorized us as something else, which we laughed about because it was kind of funny. But the NBC exit polls are anything but funny. Two, our Native identities are very complex, in that we have a racial and political relationship with the United States government. And if you're not familiar with navigating these intricacies, it makes analyzing this data very difficult, and sometimes harmful. Three, the NBC pollsters most likely did not verify the identity of those who were participating in their polls. They're alleging that someone identified themselves as American Indian, and because of the complexities of our identities, which I pointed out in point two, they had to take it as fact. And I need to point this out. The poll director for Northern Arizona University stated that polling Native American people is a particularly hard thing to do. In conclusion, I don't find the NBC exit polls accurate. There are conservative Native people who did vote for Trump, but that's a conversation for later. And if any news agencies are looking to collect meaningful data regarding Native people, please know it is a much more involved process than asking and or assuming if people are Native. I hope this information was helpful, and I genuinely hope that you're doing okay. Take care.

_transcript: Here's a great question. How do they figure the margin of error in a survey? So, for example, you have a presidential preference survey and you say, if the election were held today, would you vote for candidate A or candidate B? And A has 48% and B has 43%. Then you see a margin of error number, usually somewhere in the neighborhood of 3 to 5%. In surveys, that margin of error is to a 95% confidence interval, which means, say, there's a 3% margin of error. At the 48% number for the candidate A, there is a 95% chance that the actual preference for that candidate among everybody in the country is between 45% and 51%, 3% on either side of the 48%. And it's calculated based on the size of the survey, the number of respondents in the survey. The more respondents, the lower the margin of error. Here's where it gets kind of screwy, though. At least in a presidential election, what really matters is state by state. And even with a very large survey, say 2,000 or 3,000 people, the number of people in a given state might be very small. You might only have a handful of people from Wyoming, for example, who responded. So the margin of error of the poll for just the people in Wyoming would be enormous, as to be meaningless. So that margin of error goes up as you get into subcategories, either, say, gender or income or age, and you get a higher and higher margin of error because there are fewer people in the survey who fit into those categories. It gets even more complex and nuanced than that, but just remember, the number of people surveyed and the margin of error are directly related.

_transcript: Make sure that you write this trick down in your bound reference before the methods exams. For this question, we're told that for some sample size n, the 95% confidence interval is this interval. And then we're told that a second random sample of size 4n is taken, and for this sample size, the sample proportion is the same as the first sample, which was size n. And what you need to work out is the 95% confidence interval for this second sample. Now, the easiest way to answer this is to sketch a diagram of a normal curve, and if we draw this and have the 95% confidence interval between 0.1 and 0.2, then there's two things that you can work out from this. The first thing is the value of p-hat. p-hat is halfway between 0.1 and 0.2, so if you chuck this in your calculator, 0.1 plus 0.2 divided by 2, you're going to get p-hat is equal to 0.15. The second thing that you can work out now is the margin of error. This is the distance between p-hat and the end of the interval. And so for the first sample size, we can say that the margin of error is equal to 0.2 minus the p-hat value, 0.15, and this is equal to 0.05. Now, here's the trick that you want to write down in your bound reference. Whenever you multiply the sample size by some number, let's call this k, then the new margin of error is going to equal the old margin of error divided by the square root of k. Now, for this question, we're multiplying the original sample size by 4, and so the new margin of error is going to equal the old one, which is 0.05, divided by the square root of 4, which is equal to 2. Chuck this in your calculator, and you're going to get 0.025. And now we can answer the question, if the sample proportion is the same for both sample sizes, then it's still going to remain at 0.15.
